items.title: US House Democrats expand probe into Trump Jr.'s investments
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US House Democrats probing Donald Trump Jr.'s business dealings have sought records from prediction market firm Polymarket, vaping company Juul and two other companies tied to 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where the president's son is a partner.

In letters published on Tuesday, US Representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee next year, asked the companies — which also include GrabAGun (PEW.N) and Hadrian Automation — for a range of records of communications with 1789 Capital and its executives.

"The probe examines whether the President's son and his business partners helped steer federal contracts or regulatory decisions to companies in which they had a significant financial interest or used advance knowledge of those forthcoming decisions to make investments and profit," Raskin's office wrote in a press release. Raskin opened the probe in August.

Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, are preparing a flurry of investigations into Republican President Donald Trump and his administration, from contracts and potential conflicts of interest, to immigration and the investigation into the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

1789 Capital President Omeed Malik and Trump Jr. denied any wrongdoing at an Axios event last week.

"We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors," Bill Burck, an attorney representing 1789 Capital, said in a statement. "These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."

Juul said it intended "to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company."

A representative for online gun retailer GrabAGun said: "Congressman Raskin's letter is a political document, and its allegations are baseless."

Representatives for Trump Jr., Polymarket and Hadrian Automation did not immediately return requests for comment.

In a move legal experts say will likely face challenges, President Donald Trump sought on Friday to curb cooperation between the private sector and Congress, ordering companies with federal contracts to alert the White House before sharing information with lawmakers, and to withhold material deemed confidential.

Under the US Constitution, Congress has oversight powers and authority to obtain information, including via subpoenas that the administration has sought to limit in scope.

RASKIN HIGHLIGHTS TIMING OF INVESTMENTS

Raskin's expanded investigation focuses on how the four companies "benefited, or stand to benefit," from Trump administration contracts, regulatory decisions or proposed rule changes, which Raskin said could point to conflicts of interest or other misconduct.

In his letter to Polymarket, Raskin said that the company had effectively been banned from the US and was also under federal investigation before Trump returned to office.

In July 2025, regulators closed that probe and approved Polymarket's acquisition of a US platform that paved the way for it to re-enter the US market. The following month, Polymarket disclosed that 1789 Capital had made a strategic investment, Raskin wrote. Reuters and other outlets reported at the time that the investment was worth tens of millions of dollars.

Reuters reported last month that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has reopened its probe into Polymarket.

Raskin also said that in July 2025, months after 1789 Capital made a $5 million investment in Juul, authorities eased restrictions on sales of some Juul products, with more authorized earlier this year.

GrabAGun went public in 2025 after merging with a special-purpose acquisition company backed by Malik. In May 2026, the Trump administration proposed rules to make it easier to direct-ship guns to customers, Raskin also said.

The GrabAGun representative said the proposed rule changes were well known across the industry and that the company only provided input through the public comment process.

Raskin also wrote to Hadrian Automation, saying that the manufacturing company won US government contracts worth nearly $1 billion shortly after 1789 Capital acquired a stake in the company.

Raskin said that the president himself has publicly acknowledged the business conflicts, telling CNBC in July: "I feel badly in a way for my kids ... Almost anything they do ... they have inside information."

items.title: Radar issue delaying flights at Chicago O'Hare airport, FAA says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - An outage with a ground radar system is delaying flights into Chicago O'Hare International Airport and could force a halt to arriving flights, the US Federal Aviation Administration said on Tuesday.

The FAA said it "is temporarily delaying some flights while technicians work to repair a piece of air traffic equipment."

Air traffic control uses the ground surveillance radar and tracking system, known as ASDE-X, to monitor aircraft and vehicles on airport runways and taxiways. The FAA warned if the airport became congested, it could again temporarily halt arriving flights.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, about 13%, or 373 flights, have been delayed at the American (AAL.O) and United Airlines (UAL.O) hub on what the FAA says is the busiest day for flights during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period.

The FAA, which earlier on Tuesday had paused most arriving flights into O'Hare, said delays were averaging 47 minutes and the issue could last until 1 a.m. ET (0600 GMT) on Wednesday. The FAA said some flights were being forced to hold for up to 30 minutes in the air before landing.

The FAA and airlines have faced a series of issues since a router outage triggered a nationwide ground stop on November 13 that lasted nearly five hours and led to more than 18,000 cancelled flights and affected more than 1.5 million passengers.

Reporting by David Shepardson and Jasper Ward in Washington, editing by Chris Reese, Rod Nickel and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: US CIA, ODNI suffer cybersecurity breach of some unclassified information, source says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The US Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The intrusions affected a network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, according to the New York Times, which first reported on the breach.

While it was not clear specifically what unclassified material was compromised, information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, the Times added.

Asked about the report, the ODNI said there had been "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems."

The news is the latest in a series of tech outages and cybersecurity incidents, including a breach reported at the US Department of Agriculture. Two separate breaches have recently been disclosed at the FBI, while the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security have also been caught up in recent cyber incidents.

The Times report did not say how the breach occurred.

Reporting by Daphne Psaledakis, Christian Martinez, Ismail Shakil, and Raphael Satter; Editing by Jasper Ward, Caitlin Webber and Nick Zieminski

items.title: Nidal Hasan asks US judge for stay of execution for Fort Hood murders
items.content_html:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - Nidal Hasan, the former US Army major sentenced to be executed next week at the same Fort Hood military base where he murdered 13 people in 2009, asked a federal judge on Tuesday to halt the execution while he mounts a legal challenge to his sentence.

President Donald Trump in October approved the firing squad execution of Hasan, calling him "a very bad and evil man," while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made the unprecedented promise to livestream Hasan's death at the Texas military base. Trump scrapped Hegseth's broadcast plans after widespread outcry.

Hasan, imprisoned at the Fort Leavenworth military base in Kansas, has asked a federal judge in Topeka to issue a stay of execution, potentially delaying it by months or years.

US District Judge Anthony Mattivi ordered a hearing about the stay scheduled for Wednesday morning.

Under US law, a condemned person can seek legal review of their detention and sentence, known as a habeas corpus petition, once they have been told the date and method of their execution.

A spokesperson for the Department of Defense did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, used a laser-sighted handgun to kill 13 people in a medical facility at the sprawling Fort Hood base before he shot himself, becoming paralyzed from the chest down, and was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder by a military court-martial jury in 2013.

The US military has not carried out an execution following a court-martial conviction since 1961, and Hasan would become the first person the US military has executed by firing squad since 1945.

Of the four men on the US military's death row, only one besides Hasan has had an execution approved and scheduled by a US president: Ronald Gray was scheduled to be executed in December 2008, but his execution was indefinitely stayed by a judge through the same habeas petition Hasan is using this week.

Hasan, born in the US to Palestinian parents, represented himself at his military trial. The judge did not allow him to pursue his planned defense that the killings were justified because he was defending the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.

In his petition, Hasan said he intends to argue that being barred from advancing this defense at his trial was a violation of his constitutional rights to due process, and that Trump and Hegseth violated military rules when setting Hasan's execution date, including by promising to broadcast his death.

The motion for a stay of execution filed by lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union of Kansas said that Hasan again intends to represent himself in the habeas proceedings, where a judge will decide if his conviction and sentence were constitutional.

"There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss," Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU's Capital Punishment Project, said in a statement. "But the gravity of that loss does not change the government's obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system."

Reporting by Jonathan Allen in New York, Phil Stewart and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Stephen Coates and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: East Coast storm to bring rain, strong winds on US Thanksgiving
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Storms bringing heavy rain and winds up and down the Eastern Seaboard are threatening to delay flights during one of the busiest travel weeks of the year and could ground some of the biggest balloons in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, forecasters said on Tuesday.

Rainfall rates could reach 1 inch (2.5 cm) per hour at times, with wind gusts exceeding 50 mph (80 kph), according to the National Weather Service.

Onshore winds, king tides — the highest high-tide cycles of the year — and this week's full moon could combine to produce moderate to major coastal flooding from Georgia and the Carolinas to Long Island. At least minor coastal flooding is also forecast across coastal New England.

The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the San Francisco Bay Area through late Thursday afternoon, warning that flooding could reach 2.7 feet (0.8 meter) in some low-lying areas as near-record high tides swell the region's waterways.

Rain is expected to spread across much of the Southeast on Wednesday, potentially disrupting Thanksgiving travel for millions of Americans, before advancing into the Mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley by Wednesday night. Washington state and coastal Oregon are also forecast to see rain, with snow in the mountains.

In New York City, home to the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, conditions are expected to remain dry for the 8:30 a.m. ET (1330 GMT) start. Rain is forecast to develop by late morning or early afternoon and intensify through the evening. City rules require parade balloons to fly at lower elevations or remain grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts top 34 mph.

The Federal Aviation Administration expects the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years, with more than 417,000 flights scheduled during the nine-day window. Tuesday is forecast to be the busiest day, with 52,000 flights. The agency said in a press release that rain could affect flights across the Southeast, including Atlanta, on Wednesday before moving into the Mid-Atlantic later in the day.

Reporting by Helen Coster; editing by Donna Bryson and Aurora Ellis

items.title: Wisconsin reports third measles-related death this year
items.content_html:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - Wisconsin reported a third measles-related death on Tuesday, as the United States grapples with its worst outbreak of the viral infection in decades.

The latest death involved an adult resident of Lafayette County, the state's health department said. Wisconsin has reported 918 cases and 19 hospitalizations across 24 counties since August.

Earlier this month, the state reported its first two measles-associated deaths, involving an infant and a child from Grant County.

"This is terrible news for the nation and clear evidence that reduced vaccination rates are enabling measles to get a foothold in communities across the country," said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry.

Vaccination, he said, remains the most effective protection, particularly for young children and other vulnerable people.

The US is battling the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades, with the overwhelming majority occurring among unvaccinated people.

The country has reported 5,838 confirmed measles cases and six associated deaths in 2026, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

However, based on publicly reported state figures, the US has recorded at least 14 measles-associated deaths this year, including nine fatalities in Pennsylvania and one each in Virginia and New York state.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

Earlier this month, the US lost its hard-fought measles elimination status after 26 years as the country failed to curb the continuous spread of the highly contagious virus for more than a year.

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Reporting by Christy Santhosh and Kunal Das in Bengaluru; Editing by Vijay Kishore, Diti Pujara and Shilpi Majumdar

items.title: Thomas Markle charged in US on second count of possessing child sexual abuse material
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, and father-in-law of Britain's Prince Harry, was indicted on Tuesday in US federal court on two counts of possessing child sexual abuse material.

The indictment doubles the number of federal charges currently lodged in Los Angeles against the 82-year-old Markle in a case that grew out of an investigation initiated last month in the Philippines, where he previously resided.

The elder Markle was originally charged on November 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images.

According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question was found in two Los Angeles storage units and included two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of undress.

One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appeared to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, the affidavit said.

Philippine police said last week criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country's Cebu province, where he once lived, accusing him of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children.

Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as "sick lies."

He was arrested on November 6 at a Florida assisted-living facility where he has been a patient, and is expected to be transferred to California in the coming weeks to be arraigned in US District Court in Los Angeles on the two-count grand jury indictment returned on Tuesday.

Following a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation of Markle, a US magistrate judge in Tampa, Florida, last week ruled that he was mentally competent to stand trial, meaning that he understood the proceedings against him and could assist in his own defense.

Each count of possession of child sexual abuse material, an offense referred to in the US criminal code as possession of child pornography, is punishable by up to 20 years in prison if he is convicted, the US attorney's statement said.

Meghan Markle, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles' younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became aware of allegations against her father. She has said she was "deeply distressed" over the matter, which led her to cut off contact between her father and her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Chris Reese and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: Trump spares turkeys Freedom and Feathers from fowl Thanksgiving fate
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump has described the presidential pardon as "extreme powers." On Tuesday, he used it to spare two turkeys from the imminent threat of becoming Thanksgiving dinner.

Trump granted pardons to Freedom and Feathers, the 4-month-old fowl selected for the annual White House ritual.

Raised at Deans Gap Farm in Fort Seybert, West Virginia, the birds spent Monday night at the lavish Willard InterContinental Hotel in Washington before their White House appearance. Trump said next year's turkeys could stay overnight in the new White House state ballroom, where he said he would also hold the pardon ceremony.

Online voters selected Freedom to receive Trump's formal pardon, but both birds will retire to Texas A&M University after their reprieve.

At Tuesday's ceremony on the White House's new South Lawn helipad, Trump gazed at Freedom and noticed his companion was missing.

"Where's Feathers?" he asked.

The second turkey was resting in the White House, officials said. Trump quipped that he'd run off into the bushes.

Moments later, he rested his hand on the bird's fluffy white plumes.

"Freedom," Trump said, "I just want to say, that you and Feathers, as of this moment, have a complete and total pardon."

The tradition dates back more than a century, when poultry farmers sent turkeys to the White House as holiday gifts, forcing presidents and first ladies to coordinate avian logistics to handle the incoming birds — many of which arrived alive. In 1989, President George H.W. Bush formalized a reprieve for the birds, turning the annual turkey presentation into a pardon.

The rising cost of a Thanksgiving dinner could cast a shadow this year on Americans' turkey-centered feasts.

Holiday staples are 6% more expensive this year than 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. Turkey prices jumped more than 10%, according to the federation, which cited Department of Agriculture data on strong demand, including for exports, and low inventories.

Consumer prices for other Thanksgiving staples and ingredients, such as ham, milk, dinner rolls, sweet potatoes and cranberries, also increased.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump awarded the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, to Rudy Giuliani, his one-time personal attorney and New York mayor during the September 11, 2001, attacks on the World Trade Center buildings.

Giuliani himself was once the beneficiary of a Trump reprieve. Trump pardoned Giuliani in 2025 as he faced legal fallout for attempting to overturn the 2020 election results.

items.title: US Army sets out measures to limit lead dust from Iowa explosives blast
items.content_html:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The US Army said it was working to keep toxic lead dust to a minimum when it detonates nearly 10,000 pounds (4,500 kg) of degraded lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday, as residents sought clearer information about the risks from the blast.

The controlled blast is intended to prevent the aging explosive from detonating on its own. Residents in southeastern Iowa have struggled to keep up with changing information about where a plume of lead dust could travel after the explosion.

At a press conference on Tuesday, officials said the mitigation measures, some put in place in recent days, included a series of earthworks encircling two subsurface concrete bunkers containing the lead azide, as well as a misting apparatus to dampen the surrounding terrain and a system to flood the blast site with special foam designed to capture dust from the blast.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown was scheduled for 9 a.m. (1500 GMT) on Wednesday, when weather conditions were expected to be "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

Lead azide is an explosive chemical used to detonate military munitions. The Army brought stockpiles from installations around the country to the Iowa plant in 2009 after moving away from its use. Officials discovered dangerous crystallization during an inspection in March and have since been seeking a safe way to dispose of it.

MULTI-AGENCY RESPONSE

The Army contacted the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in March seeking guidance on the stockpile, according to ATF Director Rob Cekada.

Some of the lead azide was already more than 60 years old when it was moved to Iowa, he said.

Cekada said falling temperatures make lead azide more sensitive to shock and friction, raising the risk that it could detonate on its own.

"It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be in."

The last major disposal of lead azide was an open-air detonation of 7,000 pounds of the chemical in Colorado in 1977, Army Colonel Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, said.

Teller said that detonation occurred with "zero mitigation" and that 75% of the lead particulate remained at the incident site.

"We believe we can reduce that last 25% with the mitigation strategy that we have in place," he said.

Lead exposure can cause a range of health problems, particularly in children, in whom it can interfere with cognitive development, according to Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a public health professor at the University of Iowa. Once it settles in the environment, it does not break down, he said.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency said residents within 5 miles (8 km) of the blast may be evacuated, while those within 5 to 20 miles were advised to stay indoors with windows closed to avoid lead dust exposure.

Army projections released on Tuesday showed lead dust could settle on surfaces as far as 40 miles southwest of the blast site, extending through southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri. Airborne particles could travel nearly 100 miles within eight hours, according to the projections.

The Army said it would release updated projection maps hourly beginning six hours before the scheduled explosion and release a final estimate of the affected area afterward.

Officials said information about the problems with the lead azide stockpile had been made public and town halls had been held to inform members of the community closest to the detonation site.

The Army, however, announced the original date of November 20 detonation date only the Sunday before.

RESIDENTS SEEK ANSWERS

Some residents said changing guidance over the timing of the blast and the likely path of the lead plume had left them confused and frustrated.

Jill Holler, 51, took soil samples from her two family farms near Middletown this week so she can compare lead levels after the detonation. She's also worried about her cattle, which have no indoor shelter.

Holler welcomed the additional information released by the US Army on Tuesday but questioned why it had taken so long, noting that the detonation had originally been scheduled for last Friday.

"I'm not opposed if this is the only safe option," said Holler, who organized a protest in Middletown last week. "What I'm saying is that it's been so mishandled that people are confused and don't trust anything they're saying."

Patrick Wall, a beef field specialist with Iowa State University Extension and Outreach, said he had been fielding calls throughout the week from cattle producers seeking advice on how to protect their herds.

Wall said he only became aware of the planned detonation on November 16 and had since put together recommendations for local producers.

"Communication was probably the poorest part of how this was handled," he said.

Reporting by Renee Hickman in Chicago and Joseph Ax in New York; editing by Donna Bryson and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: China's Huawei convicted in sprawling US criminal trial over Iran business
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei was convicted by a jury in New York City on Tuesday in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it deceived banks about its business in Iran and stole trade secrets from American companies.

The verdict came in a criminal case that began in 2018, with the US government the following year placing Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology amid American concerns that Huawei posed national security risks.

The jury in Brooklyn federal court found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts the company faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets. The jury acquitted Huawei of conspiring to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging the company had acted as a criminal enterprise.

The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defense calling 15. It was not immediately clear what penalties Huawei will face when US District Judge Ann Donnelly sentences it on September 14, 2027.

Reuters stories in 2012 and 2013 helped expose Huawei's activities in Iran and were discussed during the trial.

"After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during closing arguments in the case last week.

Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, said the company was disappointed by the convictions but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge vindicated its "good-faith compliance culture."

"We fully expect to appeal," Heberlig told reporters.

US Attorney Joseph Nocella said in a statement: "Few crimes are as serious as Huawei's decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws." China's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Asked how much the company may have to pay in penalties, Heberlig said it was premature to comment, but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge could make a significant difference.

Experts have said the case did not undermine Huawei's business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China's push for artificial intelligence.

FOUNDER'S DAUGHTER WAS DETAINED

In December 2018, Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of the company's founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada.

Meng had been secretly indicted on US charges of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of American sanctions. Meng fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero's welcome. The charges against her were dropped.

Meng did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.

The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC (HSBA.L), Standard Chartered (STAN.L) and BNP Paribas (BNPP.PA) about its business dealings in Iran. Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including allegations that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.

THE PROSECUTION CASE

During the trial, prosecutors sought to prove that Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems (CSCO.O) for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel's antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.

Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile (TMUS.O) testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.

Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng's deferred prosecution agreement in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran.

The defense argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei's business in Iran and were competing for Huawei's business.

Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having "cherry-picked" a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy. Heberlig said Huawei succeeded through "hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development."

The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

Additional reporting by Luc Cohen and Jonathan Stempel; Editing by Jonathan Spicer, Noeleen Walder and Will Dunham

items.title: 'How to Kill a Federal Judge' author sentenced to 6-1/2 years in US prison for threats
items.content_html:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - A Minnesota man was sentenced on Tuesday to 6-1/2 years in prison after his conviction for writing and distributing a 236-page manuscript titled "How to Kill a Federal Judge" that threatened numerous people, including a judge who presided over an earlier, similar case against him.

US District Judge Karen Schreier during a hearing in St. Paul sentenced Robert Phillip Ivers, 73, after a jury in August found him guilty of mailing threatening communications and threatening to murder a federal judge.

Prosecutors had sought a sentence at the high end of the recommended 97- to 121-month range he faced, saying Ivers' conduct was not an isolated incident and that a message needed to be sent after the number of hostile threats and communications targeting federal judges more than tripled over a decade.

"Ivers's sentence should make crystal clear that such threats of violence cannot and will not be normalized," prosecutors in a court filing told Schreier, who sits in South Dakota but was assigned the case after all the federal judges in Minnesota recused themselves.

Ivers' court-appointed attorney did not respond to a request for comment. In court papers, he asked the judge to show Ivers leniency, citing health concerns.

Ivers, who was previously convicted of threatening to kill a federal judge in 2019, was arrested in September 2025 after staff at a library in Wayzata, Minnesota, reported seeing him print copies of his manuscript.

Prosecutors alleged Ivers gave staff a three-page flyer that described his book as a guide "designed to teach extremists on how to plan, train, hunt, stalk and kill anyone including judges, their family members, politicians and more!"

Authorities said they later found 20 spiral-bound copies of the manuscript in his car.

Prosecutors called the document a "manifesto" and said it named multiple individuals and judges. Between January and April 2025, Ivers mailed copies to all nine US Supreme Court justices, three federal appeals judges, a law firm and a university, prosecutors said.

The document included threats to kill Iowa-based US District Judge Robert Pratt, who before his death in January had, due to recusals by Minnesota judges, presided over a 2019 trial in which Ivers was convicted of threatening to kill US District Judge Wilhelmina Wright.

Pratt sentenced Ivers to 18 months in prison. Prosecutors said that Ivers' manuscript threatened Pratt as well as a lawyer who had testified to hearing Ivers threaten to kill Wright.

"Begging for your life won't do you one bit of good judge," Ivers wrote regarding Pratt, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors initially also charged Ivers with threatening to kill a Supreme Court justice but later dropped that charge.

The case is United States v. Ivers, U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, No. 25-cr-00347.

For the United States: Bradley Endicott and William Mattessich of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota

For Ivers: Glenn Bruder of Mitchell, Bruder & Johnson

Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston

items.title: Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia to leave US for Spain
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him one of the symbols of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, will leave the US for Spain on Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The departure of Abrego Garcia, 31, would bring to a close a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court. US authorities agreed to the voluntary departure as part of a negotiated deal, the Washington Post reported, citing sources.

Lawyers for Abrego Garcia did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday. Neither did the Justice Department or the Department of Homeland Security.

"The Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation," US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, the state where Abrego Garcia lived, said in a post on X on Tuesday.

US authorities sent Abrego Garcia, who entered the US illegally, to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a prior court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.

Officials called his removal an "administrative error," but for months said they could not bring him back, thrusting his case into the debate over Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation drive.

After the US Supreme Court ordered the government facilitate Abrego Garcia's return, prosecutors secured a criminal indictment charging him with human smuggling in a case stemming from an earlier incident. The Trump administration then brought Abrego Garcia back to the US in June 2025. It later attempted to deport him to Liberia after a US judge dismissed the human smuggling charge.

Human rights groups say Trump's immigration crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

The Trump administration says its actions aim to improve domestic security and are in compliance with the law.

Democrats, who won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, say they aim to hold the Trump administration accountable for its immigration policies.

items.title: Democrats aim to reverse Trump's slashes to US food aid, but path unclear
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Top Democrats in the US Congress have pledged to reverse President Donald Trump's cuts to food aid benefits when they take control of both the Senate and House in January, though their exact path to do so is unclear.

More than 5.5 million people have lost Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, also known as food stamps, since the July 2025 passage of Trump's tax law, which cut the aid program by $187 billion, or about 17%.

That declining enrollment comes as Americans face rising food costs, driven up in part by the war with Iran and high diesel prices, ahead of Thanksgiving and the winter holiday season. Food banks have reported sustained high demand ahead of the holidays.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in an email that "Senate Democrats will fight against Trump's cuts to food stamps, his tariffs, his war, and all other policies that are stretching Americans thin."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, also from New York, has said Democrats should reverse the cuts, but did not respond to a request for comment. Neither Democrat has offered specific legislative strategies they would use to reverse the cuts.

More than 200 Democratic representatives signed a November 18 letter to Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins urging her to repeal a proposed rule that would threaten SNAP benefits for 6.3 million people by curbing automatic SNAP eligibility for households receiving cash aid from a separate welfare program.

Democrats could pass legislation reversing the 2025 tax law's SNAP cuts and overturning any final USDA rule with their sizable incoming majorities in both chambers. But they will still lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override Trump's presidential veto power.

To do that, they would need significant support from Republicans, who overwhelmingly supported Trump's tax law and its cuts to SNAP.

Trump said last week that he plans to veto legislation passed by Democrats, though he signaled openness to discussion of some policies.

LEADERSHIP CHANGES

The House and Senate Agriculture Committees, which draft the farm bill and could put forward legislation to reverse SNAP cuts, will see new leadership next year.

Three members of the House committee — Vice Ranking Member Shontel Brown of Ohio, Don Davis of North Carolina and Jim Costa of California — are jockeying to replace outgoing Ranking Member Angie Craig, a fellow Democrat who is leaving Congress and who has fought Trump's SNAP cuts.

Brown said in an email that the cuts must be reversed and that they burden both Democrat- and Republican-led states.

"We can't rule in or rule out any legislative vehicle at this point because time is of the essence," Brown said.

In the US Senate, Michael Bennet of Colorado and Ohio's Sherrod Brown are vying to replace Amy Klobuchar, who is leaving to become governor of Minnesota, as top Democrat on the Agriculture Committee.

Costa, Davis, Bennet and Senator-elect Sherrod Brown did not respond to requests for comment about how they would approach reversing SNAP cuts.

Trump last week urged Congress to pass the five-year farm bill, which authorizes SNAP and is several years delayed.

Democrats have said the bill must include a two-year delay to the state cost-share provision of Trump's 2025 law, which will foist billions of dollars of spending onto states for SNAP benefits.

The Senate has yet to vote on the bill with 15 days remaining in its session.

items.title: Trump awards Rudy Giuliani the Medal of Freedom
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Tuesday awarded the Medal of Freedom, the country's highest civilian honor, to Rudy Giuliani, the former New York mayor who became a national figure after the September 11, 2001, attacks and later helped Trump try to overturn his 2020 election defeat.

Trump announced he would honor Giuliani, 82, in September 2025 shortly after the former mayor was badly injured in a car accident. Trump at the time called him "the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."

After the 9/11 attacks, Giuliani became one of the most popular figures in US politics. He launched a Republican presidential bid in 2007, and even after it failed, he remained a prominent conservative messenger.

In a statement, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales called Giuliani "a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our nation."

Trump awarded the medal in a private Oval Office ceremony.

Giuliani in a statement said he was "honored and humbled" by the medal, and credited advice from President Ronald Reagan, under whom he served as associate attorney general and a US Attorney, for guiding his public service.

"I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together," Giuliani said.

His son, former Trump administration official Andrew Giuliani, told reporters outside the White House that the ceremony was a "special" gathering in which Trump and Giuliani reminisced about their long friendship.

Their alliance deepened after Trump lost the 2020 election. Giuliani advanced falsehoods about the result and the integrity of the voting process. He held a press conference at a Philadelphia landscaping business, where he made claims that were widely rebutted, then another at the headquarters of the Republican National Committee where hair dye dribbled down his face.

His false claims came with legal consequences. He was barred from practicing law in New York, where he once served as the US Attorney in the state's southern district, and Washington, and faced criminal charges in Georgia and Arizona for attempting to subvert the 2020 election results.

Two Georgia election workers won a $148 million judgment against Giuliani in December 2023 for defamation. He "fully satisfied" the terms of the judgment in February 2025.

By the end of that year, Trump pardoned him for federal criminal offenses.

With Giuliani's medal, Trump has awarded the Medal of Freedom 27 times between his two terms. He has predominantly reserved the honor -- designated by President John F. Kennedy for "meritorious contribution" to US security or national interests, world peace or cultural endeavors -- for former athletes. Fourteen of Trump's awards have been to retired athletes, some of whom also served in public office.

He has said he plans to award the medal to retired and scandal-plagued Major League Baseball pitcher Roger Clemens and US national hockey team goaltender Connor Hellebuyck.

Trump posthumously awarded the medal to slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk in October 2025.

Reporting by Jacob Bogage; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Deepa Babington

items.title: Black Southerners say Democrats wrote them off. Their votes may have changed that.
items.content_html:
HATTIESBURG, Mississippi, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The sun rises every day over a memorial to civil rights leader Vernon Dahmer, murdered in 1966 by the Ku Klux Klan for paying poll taxes for fellow Black voters. Then at dusk, it sets on a 1910 Confederate monument, a symbol of racism to some, just yards away in Hattiesburg, Mississippi.

Melanie Sowell has renewed hope the dark legacy that has long hung over this Southern city will eventually lift.

“One day, if we continue this fight, the sun will set on the segregation, the racism and hatred that we live with every day and fight so hard to combat,” said Sowell, 57, chair of the Forrest County Democratic Party in Hattiesburg.

That hope came closer to reality when Scott Colom, a state district attorney, upset incumbent Republican US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in this month's midterm elections, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, the period after the Civil War. Colom won Forrest County, which includes Hattiesburg, by 11 percentage points, though President Donald Trump carried it by 18 points in 2024.

As in Hattiesburg, Black voters across the South helped deliver upset victories for Democrats in proportions not seen in generations.

Black political leaders and organizers have argued for years that Democrats could build lasting political power in the region if the party invested in its large Black electorate rather than writing off Republican-dominated states.

Expanded Black voter mobilization efforts offer a potential blueprint for how Democrats can strengthen their position ahead of 2028 US elections, according to interviews with more than 15 grassroots organizers, political strategists and civil rights scholars.

The question now is whether Mississippi, home to the largest share of Black residents of any state, was an anomaly or an example of a broader phenomenon: a reservoir of Black political power and a growing multiracial coalition that Democrats have underestimated.

The will is there, according to interviews with 19 Mississippi voters. Many say there is palpable energy stemming from anger and frustration that voting rights, jobs and identities are under attack.

“We have done so much to try to get power back in the hands of the people,” said Gloria McCray-Watson, 63, an academic counselor at Jackson State University in Jackson, Mississippi. “And I feel like we got sick and tired.”

UNDERINVESTMENT

For decades, many Democratic strategists have centered national plans on a narrow map of battleground states, leaving much of the South with little sustained party infrastructure or campaign investment.

Marc Morial, president of the civil rights nonprofit National Urban League, said the shift occurred after former President Bill Clinton’s 1990s campaigns, which focused on winning Black votes while also appealing to moderate and conservative white voters. Since then, the Democratic Party has made a long-term retreat from grassroots organizing, candidate recruitment and voter registration, Morial said.

Stacey Abrams, former Georgia gubernatorial candidate, and Black-led organizations spent years restarting grassroots work to turn a once reliably Republican state into a swing state. Democrats won two statewide seats in Georgia, including the governor’s race, in which Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected state governor in US history.

“Black-led organizations never stopped investing where our people are,” said Melanie Campbell, president of the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation, a nonprofit that worked with the NAACP’s “All Roads Lead to the South” voter engagement campaign along with 160 other local organizations.

In Alabama, Democratic US Representative Shomari Figures won reelection despite a dramatic redrawing of his district to make it more favorable to Republicans. Trump had carried the new areas by about 14 points in 2024.

Tennessee State Representative Justin Pearson, a Democrat, ran in a Memphis-area district that Republicans also reshaped. They pushed through a new congressional map that split the Memphis-based district into three. He lost by roughly 1.1 points.

“The important lesson to be learned here is that the Democratic Party’s future flows through the South,” Morial said. “Many of us have been saying over the years that the underinvestment meant that you would have low Black voter turnout in presidential and Senate elections.”

The party, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, defended its approach, saying Senate Democrats flipped nine seats in 2026, including seven in states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. The committee said it remained focused on expanding the map and would “work to flip every seat we can in 2028.”

“In the face of a difficult map and being massively outspent across the country, Senate Democrats made history by flipping 9 Senate seats, including 7 states Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024,” a DSCC spokesperson said in a statement.

Though Colom won his election, it came down to “affidavit ballots” — those set aside by poll workers from voters they cannot immediately verify and later counted by hand by officials in court. That process would have been unnecessary if the party invested earlier, widening its margin, according to a dozen party insiders and operatives in the state.

Canvassers in Forrest County such as Seija Hunter had to improvise with limited resources. The 39-year-old nursing assistant said she had only Colom’s name.

“When we started out, we didn’t even have any flyers, so we were going to people’s houses and people would ask us, ‘What does he look like?’” she said. “All we had was a sample ballot.”

REPUBLICANS CITE COST OF LIVING FRUSTRATION

High Black voter turnout is not the whole story, said Williamson County, Tennessee, Republican Party Chair Steve Hickey. Republican losses across the South were a culmination of voter frustration over the cost of living and failure of the party to sustain the economic message that helped Trump win a second term in 2024, he said.

NBC News exit polls show the cost of living weighed on Tennessee voters, with 82% calling it a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. Still, 51% said Republicans were better able to handle the economy, compared with 36% for Democrats.

Some Republican strategists caution against viewing Democratic gains as permanent. Diante Johnson, president of the Black Conservative Federation, said the Republican Party’s midterm defeat was driven by lower engagement from Make America Great Again supporters, diminished turnout among young men and lack of funding for conservative grassroots organizations.

“This is the first year since 2016 we did not do any door-knocking or grassroots on the ground. Grassroots has to be funded and it wasn’t funded this go around. A campaign is not a campaign without the coalitions,” Johnson said.

The coalition behind Colom extended beyond Black voters, about 97% of whom backed him, according to NBC exit poll data. About 27% of white voters backed Colom, as did about 9% of those who said they voted for Trump in 2024.

Turnout must remain high for Democrats to hold the ground they gained, said Deborah Delgado, 74, the first Black woman elected to Hattiesburg's city council. She worries that Republicans, who hold the governorship and control both chambers of the state legislature, could enact more partisan electoral maps or tighter voting restrictions.

‘ACTIVATED’ BLACK VOTERS

Leaders say much of voters' motivation came from the Trump administration’s own actions. Federal workforce cuts caused a cascade of job losses among Black voters, said CJ Rhodes, pastor of Mt. Helm Baptist Church in Jackson, Mississippi.

Coupled with the administration’s push to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programs and the Supreme Court’s decision to weaken the Voting Rights Act, Rhodes said Black voters across the state were “activated.”

Across Mississippi and South Carolina, nonpartisan voter registration group Registration Nation identified thousands of unregistered Black voters and sought to turn them into votes. It said sustained investment will be crucial.

“You can’t let people vote and then go away,” said Andrea Pringle, president of the organization.

items.title: Trump administration set to unveil new tariffs after probe on excess factory capacity, sources say
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The Trump administration is poised to imminently release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major US trading partners, three people with knowledge of the matter said on Tuesday, with new import duties on a wide range of goods expected.

The results of the investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 are expected as soon as Tuesday or Wednesday, these people said. The US Trade Representative's office is expected to propose new duties that would stack on top of previous tariffs already imposed during Trump's second term.

The duties would partly replace global import taxes struck down by the US Supreme Court in February. The administration's tariffs have in part contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the United States, and a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll following November's midterm elections showed 62% of respondents would support efforts to repeal the tariffs.

USTR has been investigating what it called evidence of excess industrial capacity in most of the US's largest trading partners. They are China, the European Union, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Bangladesh and Cambodia.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that the probe's results could be unveiled as soon as this week.

The US Trade Representative's office and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters queries about the pending tariff announcement.

USTR launched the excess capacity probe in March, along with a separate probe into weak or lax enforcement of anti-forced labor laws in 59 countries and the European Union. In July, the Trump administration imposed import duties of 10% or 12.5% on goods from those 60 trading partners.

It was unclear what tariff rates would be charged on imports, or what exemptions may be granted, the people said. The Trump administration has singled out China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity, which it says is flooding global markets with steel, aluminum, electric vehicles, appliances, solar products and other goods. China has rejected the accusations, saying its exports reflect competitive advantages.

The probe is partly directed at Chinese investment into countries in Southeast Asia, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid tariffs.

Under a US-China trade truce due to expire on January 10, the Trump administration has capped second-term tariffs on Chinese goods at 20%, in addition to duties of about 25% imposed during Trump's first term. The US has already imposed a 12.5% anti-forced labor duty on all Chinese imports, leaving only 7.5% to reach the 20% cap.

One of the people said that the 20% cap would likely be maintained as long as the trade truce is extended. If it expires, the excess capacity rate would snap to a higher level, providing incentive for Beijing to extend it.

The US and China also are working to cut tariffs on $30 billion of non-strategic imports from each side under a process known as the "Board of Trade." It is unclear how any new Section 301 duties would impact that process.

Reporting by David Lawder and Andrea Shalal; editing by David Gaffen

items.title: US lawmakers raise alarm at FAA decision to deploy aviation AI tool nationally
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - A group of two dozen House Democrats on Tuesday raised serious concerns about the Federal Aviation Administration decision to deploy a new AI tool to assist air traffic controllers nationwide on November 10, days before a major system failure.

The FAA in September began using a new software-based AI tool system in the Washington area that uses predictive analytics to improve how flights are managed after awarding an $875 million, 12-year contract to Air Space Intelligence.

The Democrats, led by Representative Rick Larsen of Washington, the ranking member of the House Transportation Committee, criticized the "sudden expansion of a largely untested system" and asked the FAA to answer a series of questions by November 30. "We have yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion," the lawmakers wrote.

The system, dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART, uses data to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.

The letter cited the nearly five-hour November 13 nationwide ground stop that led flights to be canceled for an estimated 1.5 million passengers due to an FAA telecom issue.

"The federal government is dealing with a crisis of confidence," the letter said. "Americans' faith in the aviation system is shaken. The opacity and inconsistency with which the FAA has handled the SMART rollout threatens to further undermine that trust."

The lawmakers want to know the data used by the FAA to validate SMART operations and what redundancies are in place to "ensure reliable ATC operations in the event of issues or outages impacting SMART."

The lawmakers also cited reports that the FAA may have retaliated against employees who raised safety concerns about SMART's rapid deployment.

The FAA declined comment and said it would respond directly to the lawmakers.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has called the tool essentially "dumb AI" and emphasized controllers remain in charge, not the software.

The system uses over 200 data streams, creates data visualizations, and produces scheduling recommendations for operations experts to consider passing along but does not involve active management of planes in the sky.

items.title: US malls make a holiday comeback as shoppers seek more than deals
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US mall owners and retailers are betting they can draw online shoppers with an experience they can't get from their screens: a festive day out.

Restaurants, entertainment and shared experiences are becoming increasingly important to draw shoppers to malls, surveys show, pushing brands to offer in-store deals and revamp their outlets to make the trip worthwhile.

Some 84% of Americans planning to shop over Thanksgiving weekend expect to do so in a physical store, the highest share since 2019, according to a survey by the International Council of Shopping Centers. And about 55% of US holiday shoppers plan to visit an indoor mall this season, up from roughly 50% last year, according to a separate consumer survey by real estate investment company JLL.

Brian Daniel, 55, of Grand Rapids, Michigan, said most of his shopping shifted online after the pandemic, but he has recently returned to malls, drawn partly by the experience of shopping in person.

"When I go to the mall, I'm not just in and out. I make it an evening. Shopping, dining, and a movie," Daniel said. During the holidays, he said, the music, decorations and ability to browse for gifts add to the appeal.

Refreshments are increasingly part of the shopping trip, with about 21% of respondents to JLL's survey expecting to buy a drink or food on every trip this holiday season, up from 12% last year.

"(Shoppers are) gravitating towards malls because of the depth and breadth of opportunities to shop," said Paul Chase, president of lifestyle property management at JLL. "It's important to customers or shoppers that they're going to go where they get ... the best experience."

Consumers heading for the mall expect to spend $1,357 per head during the holiday season, about 23% more than the amount budgeted by those who do not plan to visit malls, the JLL survey showed.

Shoppers expect to spend 17.3% more on dining and entertainment and 16% more on food and decorations than in the past holiday season, while planned spending on gifts is up just 3.1%, the survey showed.

THE NEW MALLRATS

Younger consumers are helping drive the shift, increasingly treating malls as a place to socialize rather than simply shop, Simon Property Group (SPG.N) CEO Eli Simon told a real estate conference in September.

Shoppers also "want to go where the best restaurants are; they want to go where the entertainment is," said Stephen Yalof, CEO of Tanger, which owns 42 shopping centers across the US and Canada, most of them outlet centers.

To lure shoppers, retailers are bolstering their in-store mall assortments while offering new experiences.

Coach (TPR.N), for example, is for the first time selling its Tabby and New York collection handbags across its outlet stores. In prior years, shoppers could only find these bags, which typically cost hundreds of dollars, in Coach's full-price retail stores.

"We're providing access to these items wherever our customer chooses to shop. That's new," said Leigh Manheim Levine, president of Coach North America. The brand realized that Gen Z shoppers "were very confused when they saw Tabby on TikTok but they didn't see it in the store," she said.

Coach has also been "fast and furiously" opening in-store cafés, Levine said. In the past two months, it has doubled the number of Coach Coffee Shops in North America to eight locations — mostly in outlet malls with limited food and beverage options.

"Customers have so many choices today, so we have to keep earning their visits by offering something they can't get online," said Nata Dvir, chief merchandising officer at department store chain Macy's (M.N). She pointed to an on-site Levi's tailoring pop-up and a custom Ralph Lauren embroidery station.

Reporting by Aishwarya Venugopal in Bengaluru and Danielle Kaye in Los Angeles; Editing by Lisa Jucca

items.title: US farm secretary pledges to fight court order halting her religious emails
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins pledged on Tuesday to challenge a court ruling that ordered her to stop sending religious emails to employees from her official account.

"We're going to fight it all the way to the Supreme Court," Rollins said in an interview on Fox News.

Several USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees sued Rollins in May, arguing she had "adopted a practice of sending increasingly proselytizing communications to the entire USDA workforce," including emails to staff on Christmas and Easter.

An Easter email from Rollins to staff read in part, "Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind," according to a copy seen by Reuters.

"And so like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for," the email continued.

The suit argued that Rollins' use of "our" and "we" to refer to the Christian faith amounted to establishing a religious preference within the agency.

On November 19, a US district judge ruled that Rollins "appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion."

Rollins "must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages," including ending religious communication if asked to do so by a colleague, said the ruling.

The administration of President Donald Trump has sought to expand the role of religion in the federal workplace, including by allowing employees to promote their religious beliefs.

The First Amendment of the US Constitution broadly prohibits the government from establishing a national religion.

Reporting by Leah Douglas in Washington, Editing by Franklin Paul and Nia Williams

items.title: US transportation secretary to testify before Congress on air traffic outage
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will testify next week before a Senate subcommittee to answer questions on the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop that led to more than 18,000 cancelled flights and disrupted travel for 1.5 million Americans.

Duffy will also face questions on Dec. 2 from the Senate Commerce aviation subcommittee on his request for $50 billion for air traffic control and airport modernization, the panel said Tuesday. Duffy boosted his request from $30 billion after the tech outage blamed on the installation of a single router at an FAA facility in Arkansas. The ground stop was the longest such incident since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.

Reporting by David Shepardson

items.title: US consumer confidence jumps to highest level in nearly two years
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US consumer confidence increased more than expected in November, touching its highest level in nearly two years, amid optimism over labor market conditions and the overall economy following this month's midterm elections.

The sharp improvement in confidence reported by the Conference Board on Tuesday was driven by respondents identifying as Democrats and Independents. Confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly.

President Donald Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress to Democrats in the November 3 elections, which were dominated by anger over the rising cost of living, blamed on tariffs on imports and the US-Israeli war with Iran. The Conference Board survey noted that "while consumers continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs, some comments cited hope for the general economy."

Economists viewed the surge in confidence as a good omen for the holiday shopping season, though the correlation between consumer spending and confidence is weak. Consumer spending has recorded two back-to-back quarters of robust growth even as confidence was in the doldrums.

"The headwinds and uncertainty generated by the midterm elections are no longer posing a risk to the economic outlook," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Time will tell whether the stock market's troubles with AI valuations will lead to a slowdown in real consumption spending, that is partly based on the wealth effect, in the final months of the year."

The Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumped to 103.3 this month, the highest level since January 2025, from a slightly upwardly revised 91.9 in October. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the index at 92.5 following a previously reported 91.7 in October. It mirrored a similar improvement in the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey.

The rise reported by the Conference Board was across all age groups and generations. Consumers with higher household incomes saw the largest improvement in confidence.

"Write-in responses in November were slightly less negative than previous months," said Fergus McCormick, a senior economist at the Conference Board.

The share of consumers saying jobs were "plentiful" soared to 30.8, the highest reading since May 2025, from 26.2 in October. The proportion viewing jobs as "hard to get" fell to 18.4. That was the lowest level since October 2025 and was down from 21.4 in October. The survey's so-called labor market differential widened to 12.4 from 4.8 last month.

This measure closely correlates to the unemployment rate in the Labor Department's employment report. The decline coincided with an acceleration in job gains in recent months. Consumers were also more upbeat about the labor market over the next six months, which bodes well for a further decline in the jobless rate.

INFLATION EXPECTATIONS ELEVATED

The unemployment rate dropped from 4.5% in November last year to 4.1% in October, though part of the decrease has been due to a smaller labor force amid retirements and the White House's immigration crackdown. Nonetheless, signs of a strengthening labor market is likely to clear the way for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again beyond December's anticipated hike as it tries to bring inflation under control.

The Conference Board's one-year median inflation expectations eased to a still-high 4.5% from 4.7% in October.

Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower as the sharp rally in AI shares following the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang fizzled. The dollar slipped against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

Despite the lingering angst over higher prices, more consumers planned to purchase motor vehicles as well as major appliances over the next six months. Some economists continued to expect consumer spending to slow down in the fourth quarter in part because of inflation eroding wage gains.

More consumers planned to buy a house over the next six months, with the share rising to a seven-month high despite elevated mortgage rates and higher home prices.

A separate report from the Federal Housing Finance Agency showed single-family house prices increased 2.5% in the 12 months through September after advancing 2.4% in August.

Mortgage rates have increased by about 130 basis points since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, data from mortgage finance firm Freddie Mac showed. The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.28% last week.

While the higher borrowing costs have dampened demand, house prices have maintained their upward trend because most homeowners have mortgage rates below 5%. That is discouraging some from selling their houses and contributing to a national housing shortage, especially of starter homes.

"We expect annual home price growth to slow to below 2% in the fourth quarter and to remain there until early 2028," said Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics. "Weaker demand due to high mortgage rates will weigh on prices, although we expect mortgage rates above 7% will also keep sellers to the sidelines."

items.title: US bill aims to clear hurdle to medication for people with opioid addiction
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - A pair of Democratic US lawmakers on Tuesday unveiled a bill aimed at improving access to buprenorphine, a medication that can effectively treat opioid addiction but is not commonly used.

The so-called BUPE for Recovery Act, authored by US Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and New York Representative Paul Tonko, is designed to remove a regulatory hurdle pharmacies face when ordering the drug, Heinrich's office told Reuters.

Drug distributors like McKesson (MCK.N) and Cardinal Health (CAH.N) are required to report suspicious orders of controlled substances to a US Drug Enforcement Administration-run database known as SORS. Flagging can result in orders being blocked.

Buprenorphine, often called bupe, is technically an opioid, and is among the drugs that must be reported, which addiction doctors have long bemoaned. "The treatment is flagged the same as the poison," Gregory Famiglio, a Pennsylvania-based addiction physician, said in an interview.

Order thresholds are not known to pharmacies, and fear of enforcement can discourage orders, experts say. A 2025 study by University of Texas researchers found that heightened monitoring led to rationing of buprenorphine and care interruptions.

Heinrich and Tonko's legislation would exempt bupe from such reporting for the duration of the US opioid public health emergency, first declared in 2017, and would require the government to study whether it needs to be re-included after.

Though the current congressional session is wrapping up, introducing the bill now "helps build awareness and momentum," a Heinrich spokesperson said.

A previous version of the bill stalled in 2024, but Democrats will control both chambers of Congress beginning January 3.

BROADER BARRIERS

Buprenorphine, shown to reduce cravings and overdose risk, has been on the market since 2002. But only 15% to 20% of Americans with addiction use medication — whether buprenorphine or other options like methadone — to treat their disease, recent US surveys have shown.

Experts attribute the low figures to stigma on the part of prescribing doctors and pharmacists, low reimbursement rates, and difficulty persuading people with addiction to get help.

Only 38.8% of US pharmacies were regularly dispensing buprenorphine as of 2023, a study by University of Southern California and UC Berkeley researchers found.

Some experts fear it will take more than legislation to get those numbers up. In the shadow of the opioid crisis, buprenorphine still carries the stigma of a substance that can be misused to get high, although academic and medical research has shown that is a rare occurrence.

"There's this fear of stocking opioids... and being implicated in overdoses," said Dima Qato, an associate professor of pharmacy at USC, and an author of the study.

items.title: US agency expects to screen 17.6 million air travelers over Thanksgiving week, down slightly
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The US Transportation Security Administration forecast on Tuesday it will screen 17.6 million air passengers during the weeklong Thanksgiving holiday travel period, down slightly from 2025.

The TSA screened about 18.1 million passengers in the seven-day Thanksgiving holiday period in 2025. The TSA expects to screen more than 3 million passengers on Sunday, which would be the first time this year it would top that figure.

The Federal Aviation Administration said separately it expects nearly 418,000 flights to operate over the nine-day holiday period it uses, the most in 16 years and exceeding the nearly 410,000 flights in the same period last year. The FAA forecasts 52,345 flights on Tuesday, the highest for any day during the period.

A nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop on November 13 attributed to the installation of a single router at a southern Arkansas FAA facility led to more than 18,000 flight cancellations and disrupted travel for more than 1 million people.

The White House has since assembled the Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team — which includes officials from the FAA, departments of Transportation and Defense, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence — to oversee travel issues.

The FAA also warned stormy weather could affect flights throughout the week.

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Rod Nickel

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: JD Vance's ties to prized Venezuelan oil contract under investigation by US Senate panel
items.content_html:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - A US Senate committee is investigating whether US Vice President JD Vance played a role in the awarding of a lucrative Venezuelan oil deal to commodities giant Vitol, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.

The investigation follows an exclusive Reuters report that detailed a meeting between Vance and Vitol trader John Addison a week before the United States invaded Venezuela in January and captured authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro.

"I write today with serious concern that you may have used your position as Vice President to help a major political donor secure lucrative business opportunities involving Venezuelan oil," according to the letter, sent to Vance by Senator Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat.

Hassan will become chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in January when the new Congress is seated. She's seeking a number of documents from Vance's office by December 14. Among them are communications between Vance or his staff and Addison or the trading firm.

The meeting between Vance and Addison happened in December 2025 during a trip Vance made to Montana's Yellowstone Club, an ultra-exclusive ski and golf resort, according to a person familiar with the matter. At the time, Addison was a gasoline trader for Vitol with no expertise in trading Venezuelan crude, according to Vitol. He retired from Vitol earlier this year.

Vance and Addison talked about Venezuela, according to the person with knowledge of the meeting, who was given an account of the discussion by Addison. Vance was particularly interested to know how quickly Venezuelan crude could be sold if the US hypothetically gained control of the country's oil supplies, the person said. Addison assured Vance that Vitol was well-placed to do that job.

Both Vance and Addison have denied having the meeting.

Hassan wrote in her letter: "Despite denials from your office and Mr. Addison, flight records place his private jet and your government plane at the same Montana airport on the day of the reported meeting."

In response to questions for this story, Vance's press secretary, Luke Schroeder, said in a statement: "The alleged airport meeting never happened."

Reuters did not specify, in the original report, that the meeting happened at the airport.

Vitol and Addison were not immediately available for comment.

Addison has confirmed to Reuters that on January 5 – two days after the operation that ousted Maduro and killed up to 100 people – US Energy Secretary Chris Wright called him at his desk in Houston with an irresistible offer.

President Donald Trump's administration was planning to start selling the South American OPEC nation's crude to global buyers to finance its coming political transition. Wright wanted to know from Addison if Vitol wanted the job.

The Department of Energy confirmed Wright called Addison on January 5 to discuss Venezuela.

Within days, Vitol and its rival trading firm Trafigura landed special licenses to sell Venezuela's oil, according to the two firms. The companies have since earned hundreds of millions of dollars marketing the crude, according to estimates by independent experts.

The United States handled more than $12 billion of Venezuela's oil revenue in the first nine months of this year, according to a report made public by the State Department earlier this month.

Addison had been an early backer of Vance, contributing $300,000 in 2022 to the Protect Ohio Values Political Action Committee to help Vance's successful bid for one of Ohio's US Senate seats, Federal Election Commission records show.

Later, Addison and his wife, Shannon, contributed $7 million in 2024 to political action committees to help secure Trump's second term in the White House, according to Federal Election Commission records.

Reporting By Tim McLaughlin; Editing by Anna Driver
